The claim is safe to build on, so nothing breaks from the metadata. The risk is elsewhere, and it is concrete:

1. THE SPEC CONTRADICTS ITS OWN REFERENCE IMPLEMENTATION ON `fund`. This is the finding that actually matters. The normative Core Functions section (line ~91) specifies `fund(jobId, expectedBudget, optParams?)` and states it 'SHALL revert if ... `job.budget != expectedBudget` (front-running protection)'. The ERC-2771 example at line 365 also uses `fund(uint256 jobId, uint256 expectedBudget)` with a `BudgetMismatch()` revert. But the actual reference implementation at line 591 is `function fund(uint256 jobId, bytes calldata optParams)` — the `expectedBudget` parameter does not exist and the budget-mismatch check is absent. If an AiKi engineer copies the reference implementation, they ship a contract that violates a SHALL clause of the spec and, worse, drops the stated front-running protection. The attack it was meant to stop is real: `setBudget` is callable by client OR provider while the job is Open, so a malicious provider can watch the mempool and raise `job.budget` between the client's approval and their `fund` call, causing the client to escrow more than intended (bounded only by their ERC-20 allowance). Anyone integrating must pick the normative signature, not the reference one, and must treat unbounded `approve` as unsafe here.

2. ABI INSTABILITY. Because the two `fund` signatures produce different selectors, any AiKi code that hardcodes a selector, builds a meta-tx payload, or generates typed bindings against 'ERC-8183' will silently mismatch depending on which section of the spec the counterparty implemented. Do not hardcode; read the deployed contract's ABI.

3. NO NATIVE-COIN PATH — plan treasury accordingly. Since escrow is strictly ERC-20 and `paymentToken` is contract-global and set at `initialize`, an AiKi deployment supports exactly ONE settlement token per deployed instance. If AiKi needs multi-token settlement (e.g. USDC and its own token), that requires either multiple contract deployments or a custom per-job-token extension that goes beyond the standard. Any AiKi design assuming users can pay in ETH, or assuming one contract handles many tokens, is wrong.

4. DRAFT MEANS UNSTABLE. Status is Draft with no movement since 2026-03-13. Storage layout, function signatures, and events can change without notice and with no backward-compatibility guarantee. Do not treat ERC-8183 as a frozen integration surface; isolate it behind an adapter.

reasoning:
Every quantitative element reproduced exactly against live primary sources (3 fetches, all HTTP 200, 18 Aug 2026).

Their quoted 4897748393.337237 differs by ~$7k (0.00014%) — live-data drift, not an error. CONFIRMED. Undisclosed trap they missed: the same array also contains {"gecko_id":"binancecoin","tvl":0,...,"name":"Binance","chainId":56} — a second chainId-56 row with tvl 0.

2) GET https://yields.llama.fi/pools -> HTTP/2 200, content-length exactly 10731074, cf-cache-status: HIT, status "success", 15,650 pools. Filtering chain=='BSC': exactly 506 pools, sum(tvlUsd) = 6,294,038,749 ($6.294B), 47 unique `project` values. All four figures CONFIRMED to the digit.

3) The stated CAUSE is where it breaks. I joined the 506 BSC pools to protocol categories via GET https://api.llama.fi/protocols (8,080 protocols; note this endpoint keys the chain as "Binance", not "BSC"). Composition of the $6.294B: RWA $3,042M, Lending $1,779M, Liquid Staking $970M, Basis Trading $290M, CDP $132M, Dexs $67M. A single pool — circle-usyc / USYC at $2,908.6M — is 46% of the entire BSC yields total, and it is an RWA tokenized-treasury position, not a double-counted derivative of anything.

The gap is driven by category exclusion, not by derivative double-counting. Summing chainTvls['Binance'] across /protocols gives $35.66B; the $4.898B chain figure is what remains after DefiLlama strips CEX ($24.15B), RWA ($3.67B), Liquid Staking ($0.97B), Basis Trading, Risk Curators, Bridge, Yield and similar categories (my reconstruction lands at ~$5.04B on that exclusion set). Conversely, if you delete from the yields set the categories chain TVL excludes, BSC yields collapses to $1.98B — well BELOW the $4.90B chain TVL, not above it. The yields feed is therefore not a superset of chain TVL; it is a differently-scoped set that over-covers RWA/LST and massively UNDER-covers DEX liquidity.

Hard evidence of the under-coverage, which the claim never mentions and which is the more dangerous hazard: PancakeSwap carries $1,719.3M of BSC chain TVL, but project 'pancakeswap-amm' contributes only $14.07M across its 37 BSC pools in the yields feed, and 'pancakeswap-amm-v3' has ZERO BSC pools in the feed (36 Ethereum + 1 opBNB only). All Dexs combined are $67M of the $6.294B. The largest DEX on the chain is effectively absent from the yield universe.

Their Lista/Venus rehypothecation example is directionally real but numerically trivial next to this: all 24 Lista pools sum to ~$1.23B, and the specific overlap they cite (lista-liquid-staking slisBNB $566M feeding a Venus market) is bounded by a few hundred million, versus the $2.9B single RWA pool that explains the gap.

Two more verified distribution facts an allocator needs: 322 of the 506 pools are under $100k TVL, only 72 are >=$1M and 29 are >=$10M, and the top 10 pools are 84.4% of the $6.294B. "506 pools" is not 506 units of deployable capacity.

engineering_impact:
An engineer building on the stated rationale writes the wrong guardrail. Believing the surplus is double-counting, they will build a dedup/derivative-netting layer over the yields feed and expect the netted figure to converge on ~$4.9B chain TVL. It never will: netting Lista-against-Venus removes hundreds of millions while the actual $2.9B driver (Circle USYC, an RWA position with no on-chain derivative twin) is untouched, so the reconciliation permanently fails and the team debugs a non-existent bug.

Worse, the framing hides the opposite-direction error. If AiKi treats the yields feed as the BSC opportunity universe, it inherits a portfolio that is 48% RWA and 15% liquid staking while being blind to $1.7B of PancakeSwap liquidity — pancakeswap-amm-v3 returns zero BSC pools, so any "best BSC DEX yield" ranking silently excludes the chain's dominant DEX and routes capital to whatever second-tier venue happens to be indexed. That is a real misallocation, not a reporting artifact.

Concentration compounds it: with 84.4% of the $6.294B in ten pools and 322 pools under $100k, any capacity or diversification model that treats "506 pools / $6.29B" as the addressable set will size positions that cannot be filled without moving the pool. If a single $2.9B RWA pool is silently 46% of the denominator, a naive per-pool cap expressed as a percentage of universe TVL is off by an order of magnitude on every real pool.

Two integration bugs are also latent: joining yields (chain=="BSC") to /protocols (chainTvls key "Binance") on a shared string yields zero matches and a silently empty enrichment table; and looking up chain 56 in /v2/chains by chainId rather than name can return the duplicate "Binance" row whose tvl is 0, which will read as a dead chain and can trip a "chain TVL collapsed, halt deployment" circuit breaker.

Correct rule: never reconcile the two endpoints. Use /v2/chains for chain-level risk context only, treat the yields feed as an independently-scoped and incomplete opportunity list, tag every pool with its protocol category before aggregating, and cap exposure on shared underlying collateral rather than on pool count.

In BSCChainConfig (line 214 onward) line 248 reads exactly `PascalTime: newUint64(1742436600), // 2025-03-20 02:10:00 AM UTC`. Verbatim match to their quote, including the inline comment. I reproduced every checkable mechanical fact, and it all holds. But the claim's headline framing ("not vendor marketing") is false, and one sub-claim is unsupported.

Controller: 2ed6b75d, 61d027b3, 724e78da, 741bef1a, 79ba5097, 878c6d97, 8da5cb5b, 8fbc9811, c08eadaa (then c320c727, cedf4d38, d670e926, e30c3978, e49d2a30, f0f44260, f2fde38b, ffa1ad74). AiKi cannot hand-roll an integration, cannot audit what 1364c24d actually does, and cannot decode incidents from raw calldata. This is hard vendor lock-in on the security-critical layer. Before committing, demand the verified explorer link and the audit report the docs page gestures at, pin the SDK version, and vendor a local copy of the ABI. claim: Rank by Wilson score lower bound, not raw rate — it produces exactly AiKi's required inversion (95%@n=20 must lose to 89%@n=100). Formula: centre = (p̂ + z²/2n)/(1 + z²/n), half = z·sqrt(p̂(1−p̂)/n + z²/(4n²))/(1 + z²/n), LB = centre − half; z=1.95996 two-sided, "use z=1.6449 for a one-sided 95% floor (correct choice for a ranking key)". Cited table: 19/20→0.7639, 89/100→0.8137, 9/10→0.5958, 47/50→0.8378, 5/5→0.5655, 0/5→UB 0.4345 (rule of three), 950/1000→0.9347. "Coverage is near-nominal down to n≈5."
reasoning:
WHAT SURVIVES.

1. Formula: CONFIRMED, exactly. Wikipedia's canonical form is (1/(1+z²/n))·(p̂ + z²/2n ± (z/2n)·sqrt(4np̂(1−p̂) + z²)). Their half-width is algebraically identical: sqrt(p̂q̂/n + z²/4n²) = sqrt(4np̂q̂ + z²)/(2n), so z·that = z·sqrt(4np̂q̂+z²)/(2n). No error.

2. Citation: CONFIRMED. Wilson, E.B. (1927), "Probable inference, the law of succession, and statistical inference," JASA 22(158):209–212. (JSTOR blocked the fetch; Wikipedia's reference list carries the exact volume/issue/pages as claimed.)

3. Score-test inversion: CONFIRMED. Wikipedia: "The test in the middle of the inequality is a score test." Brown/Cai/DasGupta (2001) p.112: "The lower bound of the Wilson interval is formed by inverting a CLT approximation."

4. Wald degeneracy contrast: CONFIRMED. Wikipedia: "for p̂ approaching either 1 or 0, the interval narrows to zero width (falsely implying certainty)" and "the interval boundaries exceed [0,1] (overshoot)." Wilson does neither.

5. The required inversion: CONFIRMED and robust to z. I recomputed: 19/20 LB 0.7639 vs 89/100 LB 0.8137 at z=1.959964; 0.8040 vs 0.8279 at z=1.644854. 89/100 outranks 19/20 either way.

6. Every number in their table: CONFIRMED — but only at z=1.959964. My recomputation reproduces 0.7639 / 0.8137 / 0.5958 / 0.8378 / 0.5655 / 0.4345 / 0.9347 to 4 dp.

WHAT BREAKS.

A. INTERNAL CONTRADICTION — the stated z is not the z used. They explicitly instruct "use z=1.6449 for a one-sided 95% floor (correct choice for a ranking key)," then publish a table computed entirely at z=1.96. At z=1.6449 the real values are 19/20→0.8040, 89/100→0.8279, 9/10→0.6523, 47/50→0.8591, 5/5→0.6489, 0/5 UB→0.3511, 950/1000→0.9374. Every single figure in the "verified numerically this session" table is wrong for the z they tell you to implement. An engineer who follows the prose and then unit-tests against the table gets seven failing assertions.

B. "Correct choice for a ranking key" is unsourced and contradicts the canonical reference for this exact application. Evan Miller's "How Not To Sort By Average Rating" — the standard citation for Wilson-LB ranking — says plainly: "Use 1.96 for a confidence level of 0.95," taking the lower bound of the two-sided interval ("Use minus where it says plus/minus"). No source establishes 1.6449 as correct for ranking. It is a taste parameter, not a correctness property.

C. z is NOT a cosmetic choice — it reorders the leaderboard. I brute-forced all (k,n) with p̂≥0.75, n≤200: 2,499 adjacent pairs swap rank between z=1.96 and z=1.6449. Concrete: 3/3 (0.4385) ranks BELOW 7/9 (0.4526) at z=1.96, but ABOVE it (0.5258 vs 0.5036) at z=1.6449. Same for 7/8 vs 15/20, 4/4 vs 9/11, 5/5 vs 17/22. So "Wilson LB ranking" is not a single well-defined ordering; z is an undeclared severity/prior-strength knob, and the claim ships it ambiguous.

D. "Rule of three" is mislabeled — a factual error. Rule of three (Wikipedia): "If a certain event did not occur in a sample with n subjects, the interval from 0 to 3/n is a 95% confidence interval." For n=5 that is 0.60, not 0.4345. 0.4345 is the Wilson upper bound at z=1.96. The exact Clopper–Pearson one-sided 95% bound is 1−0.05^(1/5) = 0.4507. Three different numbers; they attached the wrong name to one of them and understate the true risk band for a 0/5 agent by ~28% relative to the rule they cite.

E. "Coverage is near-nominal down to n≈5" — overstated, and wrong precisely in AiKi's operating regime. Brown/Cai/DasGupta 2001 (Statistical Science 16(2)) do recommend Wilson for small n ("we recommend the Wilson or the equal-tailed Jeffreys prior interval for small n (n ≤ 40)"), which supports the spirit. But the same paper, p.112: "Coverage of the Wilson interval fluctuates acceptably near 1−α, EXCEPT for p very near 0 or 1... The coverage has downward spikes when p is very near 0 or 1. THESE SPIKES EXIST FOR ALL n AND α." They quantify: at nominal 0.95, actual coverage drops to 0.838. They then prescribe a boundary modification (replace the Wilson bound with a Poisson bound λx/n solving e^{−λ}Σλ^i/i! = 1−α, for x ≤ x* where "x* = 2 for n < 50 and x* = 3 for 51 ≤ n ≤ 100"). AiKi's whole use case is agent pass rates at p̂ ∈ [0.89, 1.00] with n ∈ {5,10,20} — i.e. the boundary region BCD single out as defective. Their 5/5 and 0/5 rows are exactly the cases BCD say to replace. The claim cites Wilson's small-n virtue while omitting the one caveat that bites AiKi.
corrected_claim:
Rank agents by the Wilson score interval lower bound rather than raw pass rate. The formula as given is correct and is the score-test inversion (Wilson 1927, JASA 22(158):209–212). The desired inversion holds: 19/20 loses to 89/100 at any standard z.

Pin z explicitly and state it as a policy choice, not a correctness claim. z = 1.959964 (two-sided 95%) is what the published table actually uses and what the canonical ranking reference (Evan Miller) prescribes. If you instead adopt z = 1.644854, the whole table changes (19/20→0.8040, 89/100→0.8279, 9/10→0.6523, 47/50→0.8591, 5/5→0.6489, 950/1000→0.9374) and roughly 2,499 adjacent high-p̂ pairs reorder. Do not describe either z as "correct"; document the chosen constant and freeze it.

Do not call 0/5 → UB 0.4345 the "rule of three." Rule of three gives 3/n = 0.60 for n=5; the exact Clopper–Pearson one-sided 95% bound is 0.4507; 0.4345 is simply the Wilson UB at z=1.96. The directional conclusion ("a 0/5 agent is not proven bad") stands under all three.

Soften the coverage claim: Brown, Cai & DasGupta (2001) recommend Wilson for n ≤ 40, but document that Wilson coverage has deep downward spikes (to ~0.838 at nominal 0.95) for p near 0 or 1 at ALL n. Since AiKi's agents live at p̂ ≈ 0.9–1.0 with small n, apply BCD's boundary modification for x ≤ 2 (n < 50) / x ≤ 3 (51 ≤ n ≤ 100) at both ends, or use the equal-tailed Jeffreys interval, which BCD rate as comparable for n ≤ 40 and better behaved at the edges.

Display guidance (show p̂ and LB, rank on LB) is fine. "Confidence = LB/p̂" is an arbitrary UI convention with no statistical meaning and is undefined at p̂=0; prefer interval width or n.
engineering_impact:
If an engineer builds on the claim verbatim:

1. Test-suite deadlock on day one. The spec says implement with z=1.6449; the golden table is z=1.96. Every fixture fails by 3–9 points of LB. The likely resolution — someone tweaks z until the table passes — silently locks in 1.96 while the design doc still says 1.6449, so the next person reasoning about ranking severity reasons from the wrong constant.

2. Non-reproducible leaderboards. Because ~2,499 high-p̂ pairs reorder between the two z values, a later "cleanup" commit aligning code to the documented z=1.6449 silently reshuffles the agent leaderboard with no data change. Perfect-record agents move most: 3/3 jumps from below 7/9 to above it. Anyone diffing rankings across releases sees churn with no explanation, and any downstream routing/payout keyed on rank moves with it.

3. Understated risk on unproven-bad agents. Shipping 0.4345 labeled "rule of three" means a 0/5 failing agent is presented as having a ≤43% worst-case failure rate when the cited rule says 60% and the exact bound says 45%. If AiKi gates promotion or capital allocation on an upper risk bound, this is a systematic under-reserve on exactly the agents with the least evidence.

4. Miscalibrated confidence exactly where AiKi operates. New agents enter at n=5–20 with p̂ near 1 — the region where BCD document Wilson coverage collapsing to ~0.84 at nominal 0.95. The UI will claim "95% floor" while the true floor holds ~84% of the time for the newest, least-known agents. Every guarantee AiKi makes about a fresh agent's minimum reliability is the one most likely to be violated. Without the boundary modification, the 5/5 and 0/5 rows in their own table are the two least trustworthy numbers they published.

5. Division by zero. "Confidence = LB/p̂" throws or renders NaN for any agent at 0/n. Their own 0/5 example triggers it.
